summary: Brush is a Gaussian splat reconstruction engine written in Rust on the Burn machine-learning framework, licensed Apache-2.0, and it is the one trainer in this group that actually runs where the pictures are taken: the same code trains on Windows, macOS and Linux, on AMD, Intel and NVIDIA cards, on an Android phone, and inside a browser tab, because it targets WebGPU rather than CUDA. It takes a COLMAP or Nerfstudio dataset in and writes a splat PLY out, reads back both plain and SuperSplat-compressed PLY, streams a splat from a web address while it loads, and can bake several decimated levels of one scene as separate files. For a standards audience the interesting parts are at the edges. Time exists only as playback: a folder or zip of numbered PLY files, or a private 'PLY with delta frames' variant written for two research projects, neither of which is a published format. The coordinate frame is the input's frame and nothing in the exported file says which frame that is, a point the release notes state plainly. There is no scale, no licence field, no authorship record and no mesh: what comes out is a cloud of Gaussians and nothing else, so every question about rights, units and provenance is left to whatever carries the file. The project is a fork of a Google Research repository and says in its own README that it is not an official Google product.

coverage.note: Brush carries a complete splat rasteriser of its own, written against WebGPU and driven by the Burn framework, with its own radix sort and a mip filter borrowed from Mip-Splatting. What it does not carry is anything above one draw: no render graph, no pass structure, and no place for ordinary geometry beside the splats.
